subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Assalaamu alaykum, young scientist! Open your eyes and look around you right now. What do you see? Perhaps the warm golden sunshine pouring through your window, the glow of a lamp, or the pages of this very lesson. You can see all of these things because of one amazing thing called light. In this unit you will become a real light explorer. You will discover where light comes from, why we cannot see in the dark, how shadows are made, and how a shiny mirror can bounce light back to your eyes.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Identify different light sources including the sun
Know that darkness is the absence of light
Model how the spin of the Earth leads to day and night, e.g. with different sized balls and a torch

objectives.subStrand: Obtain and present evidence; Consider evidence and approach

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to reach these learning goals. Read them now, and read them again at the end to see how much you have grown as a scientist.
Name many light sources around you and say whether each one is natural or made by people.
Explain that we need light to see objects, and that in complete darkness we cannot see at all.
Describe what darkness is — it is not a thing by itself, it is simply what happens when light is missing or blocked.
Show how a shadow forms when an object blocks light, and explain what makes a shadow bigger, smaller, or point in a different direction.
Explain reflection — how light bounces off smooth, shiny surfaces such as mirrors and calm water.
Explain day and night as the result of the sun lighting one side of the spinning Earth.
Follow light safety rules, especially the golden rule of never looking straight at the sun.
Carry out simple, safe investigations about light using things from your own home.

Here are the important words for this unit. A good scientist learns to use the right words, just as a good carpenter learns the names of every tool. Read each word, its meaning, and the example. You will meet all of these words again inside the lesson.

concepts.title: What Is Light and Where Does It Come From?
concepts.explanation:
Let us start with a big and simple idea. Light is a kind of energy that lets us see. Without light, the world would be completely dark and we would not be able to see anything at all — not our mothers, not our food, not even our own hands. Light is so ordinary that we often forget how special it is. But stop and think: every colour you have ever seen, every face you love, every beautiful sunset over the Indian Ocean, reached your eyes because of light.

Some objects make their own light. We call these objects light sources. A light source is special because the light comes out of it. The most important light source of all is the sun. The sun is a giant ball of hot, glowing gas in the sky. It is really a star, the closest star to us. The sun gives light to the whole Earth. It lights up the savanna, the coral reefs, the busy streets of Nairobi and Mogadishu, and the quiet villages by the Jubba River. Without the sun, there would be no daytime, no warmth, and no plants growing for the goats and cattle to eat.

Light sources can be sorted into two groups. Natural light sources are made by nature. The sun is a natural light source. So are the stars that sparkle over the desert at night, the bright flash of lightning during the wet season, and the orange flames of a fire. Artificial light sources are made by people. When you switch on an electric light bulb, shine a torch, or light a candle, you are using artificial light. People invented artificial light so they could see at night and in dark places where sunlight cannot reach, such as inside a room with the curtains closed.

Here is a tricky question that fools many people. Is the moon a light source? It looks so bright in the night sky! But the answer is no. The moon does not make its own light. Instead, sunlight travels to the moon, and the moon reflects that light back to us, like a giant mirror in the sky. This is why the moon seems to change shape through the lunar month, growing from a thin curve to a full round circle and back again. The Islamic calendar follows these moon shapes, which is how your family knows when the blessed month of Ramadan begins and ends. So the moon is not a light source, even though it lights up the night. It is a reflector, and you will learn much more about reflection later in this lesson.
concepts.example: Light has one more secret you should know. Light travels in straight lines, and it travels very, very fast — faster than anything else in the whole universe. When you shine a torch across a dusty room, you can sometimes see the beam going in a straight path. When sunlight comes through a small gap in the clouds, it makes straight golden rays reaching down to the ground. Because light moves in straight lines, it cannot bend around corners on its own. This one idea will help you understand shadows and reflection, so keep it in your mind like a treasure.

concepts.title: Darkness Is the Absence of Light
concepts.explanation:
Now let us think about the opposite of light: darkness. Many children believe that darkness is a thing that arrives, like a dark cloud that fills a room. But that is not true, and understanding the truth is an important science idea. Darkness is not a thing at all. Darkness is simply what we call a place where there is little or no light. When the light leaves, darkness is what is left behind.

Think about a cupboard in your home. When the door is open and the room is bright, you can see the tins and bags inside. When you close the door, the inside becomes dark. Did darkness sneak in through a hole? No. The darkness happened because you blocked the light from getting in. Open the door again, and the light rushes back and the darkness disappears at once. Darkness cannot fight against light. Even a tiny candle can push away the darkness in a large room, but no amount of darkness can push away a candle's flame. Light always wins.

Darkness happens naturally too. At night, when your side of the Earth turns away from the sun, the sunlight can no longer reach you, and so it becomes dark. Deep inside a cave, where sunlight cannot travel, it is dark even in the middle of the day. At the very bottom of the deep ocean, far below the coral reefs, it is always dark because sunlight cannot reach down that far. In all these places, darkness is not something that was added. It is light that is missing.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Some animals are perfectly happy in the dark. Bats fly at night and find their way using sound instead of light. Owls have huge eyes that gather even the tiny bit of moonlight so they can hunt in the dark. Deep-sea fish live where no sunlight ever reaches, and some of them even make their own light inside their bodies to glow like little lamps!

concepts.title: How We See Objects
concepts.explanation:
Here is one of the most surprising ideas in this whole unit. How do your eyes actually see things? Many people think their eyes work like torches, sending out a beam that touches objects. That is not how seeing works. The truth is the other way around. Light from a source travels to an object, bounces off it, and then travels into your eyes. Your eyes catch the light, and that is how you see.

Let us follow the path of light with an example. Imagine Amina is holding a bright red mango in the sunshine. First, light leaves the sun. It travels down to the mango. Some of that light bounces off the mango and travels into Amina's eyes. Only then does Amina see the mango. So the light makes a journey: from the sun, to the mango, to the eye. If we take away the light, the journey cannot happen, and Amina cannot see the mango even if it is right in front of her nose.
concepts.example: This explains something you already know from your own life. In a bright room you can see everything clearly. As the room gets dimmer, you can see less and less. In complete darkness you cannot see at all, no matter how hard you try or how wide you open your eyes. This is not because your eyes stopped working. It is because there is no light bouncing off the objects into your eyes. Your eyes need light the same way a well needs water — without it, they simply cannot do their job.

concepts.title: Shadows and How They Form
concepts.explanation:
Shadows are one of the most fun parts of studying light, and you can play with them almost anywhere. A shadow is a dark shape that appears when an object blocks the light. Remember that light travels in straight lines. When something solid stands in the way, the light cannot pass through it or bend around it. So behind the object there is a patch where the light did not reach, and that patch is the shadow.

To make a shadow, you always need three things working together. First, you need a light source, such as the sun or a torch. Second, you need an opaque object — opaque means something that blocks light, like your hand, a book, or the trunk of an acacia tree. Third, you need a surface for the shadow to fall on, such as the ground, a wall, or the floor. If any one of these three is missing, there can be no shadow. Take away the light and everything is dark with no shadow. Take away the object and the light reaches the surface with nothing to block it. Take away the surface and there is nowhere for the shadow to land.

Not every material makes a strong shadow. Opaque materials, like wood, stone, metal, and your own body, block light completely and make dark, clear shadows. Transparent materials, like clean glass or clear water, let light pass straight through, so they make almost no shadow at all. That is why you can see through a glass of water but not through a wooden door. When you hold a thin cloth up to the light, some light gets through and some is blocked, so it makes a faint, soft shadow — materials like this are called translucent, which means they let a little light through.

Shadows also change their size and shape, and you can control this. When you move a torch closer to an object, the shadow grows bigger. When you move the torch farther away, the shadow gets smaller. You can test this yourself with a torch and a toy. The position of the light also decides where the shadow points. The shadow always falls on the opposite side of the object from the light. If the light is on the left, the shadow stretches to the right. This is why your own shadow outside changes through the day as the sun moves across the sky.

In the early morning, when the sun is low in the eastern sky, your shadow is very long and stretches far across the ground. At midday, when the sun is high overhead, your shadow becomes short and hides almost under your feet. In the evening, as the sun sinks low in the west, your shadow grows long again but points the other way. Long ago, before clocks and phones, clever people used these changing shadows to tell the time of day. They built simple shadow clocks called sundials, and you could make one too.
concepts.example: Did You Know? The tall acacia trees on the savanna give welcome shade to animals during the hottest part of the day. Elephants, giraffes, camels, and cattle all rest in the cool shadows to escape the strong midday sun. A shadow is really a place where the sunlight has been blocked, so it is cooler there. That is why sitting under a tree feels so pleasant on a hot afternoon!

concepts.title: Reflection and Mirrors
concepts.explanation:
You already learned that we see objects because light bounces off them into our eyes. When light bounces off a surface, we call it reflection. All objects reflect a little light, which is why we can see them. But some surfaces are especially good at reflecting light. Smooth, shiny surfaces like a mirror, a polished metal spoon, or the calm surface of water reflect light so well that they can show a clear picture, called an image.

Why do mirrors work so well while a rough wall does not? The secret is smoothness. When light hits a smooth mirror, all the light bounces off in a neat, orderly way, keeping the picture together, so you see a clear reflection of your face. When light hits a rough or bumpy surface, like sand or bark or a stone wall, the light scatters in many different directions and the picture is broken up. That is why you cannot see your face in a wall, but you can see it in a mirror or in a still pool of water. Dark surfaces reflect very little light, which is why you cannot see yourself in a piece of dark cloth.

You can see reflection in nature too. When Hassan looks into a calm well or a still pond in the early morning, he can see the sky and his own face looking back at him. But if the wind blows and makes ripples on the water, the reflection breaks apart and becomes wobbly. This happens because the water is no longer smooth. The same light is there, but the bumpy surface scatters it. This is a wonderful example of how the smoothness of a surface changes how well it reflects.
concepts.example: People use reflection in many clever and helpful ways. A car has mirrors so the driver can see what is behind without turning around. A dentist uses a tiny mirror to see the hidden back of your teeth. A periscope uses two mirrors so a person can see over a tall wall or fence. People even use shiny mirrors to flash sunlight and signal for help when they are lost. Understanding reflection is not only interesting — it can also keep people safe.

concepts.title: Day and Night
concepts.explanation:
Now let us put our light knowledge together to understand something that happens every single day of your life: day and night. During the day it is bright and we can see easily. During the night it is dark and we often need a lamp or torch. Why does this happen? It is all because of the sun and the spinning Earth.

The Earth is shaped like a giant ball, and it is always slowly spinning, like a top. The sun can only light up one half of the ball at a time — the half that is facing it. When your part of the Earth is turned toward the sun, sunlight reaches you and it is day. As the Earth keeps spinning, your part slowly turns away from the sun. The sunlight can no longer reach you, and so it becomes night. The Earth takes one whole day and night to spin around once, which is why we get one daytime and one night-time every single day.

This is why the sun seems to rise in the east each morning and set in the west each evening. The sun is not really travelling across the sky. It is the Earth that is turning, carrying you around with it. When Khadija in Hargeisa is enjoying bright afternoon sunshine, children on the other side of the world are fast asleep in the dark of night. When it becomes night for you, it is becoming day for them. Understanding this helps you see that day and night are simply about which side of our spinning Earth is facing our great light source, the sun.
concepts.example: The pattern of day and night is wonderfully dependable, and people all over East Africa build their lives around it. A farmer near Garissa wakes at sunrise to lead the cattle to water while it is cool. A trader in the Eastleigh market opens the shop in the bright morning light and closes when the sun goes down. A fisherman in Berbera or Lamu reads the colours of the sunset over the sea to plan the next day. When the sun sinks and the sky darkens, families gather, share a meal of bariis and goat meat, and light a lamp or torch so they can see. The same spinning Earth that gives you your bright school day gives every living thing its rest at night. Even the plants follow this rhythm, opening their leaves to the daytime sun and resting in the cool dark. When you understand the science of light, you begin to notice these gentle patterns of creation everywhere, from the smallest shadow on the ground to the great sun that lights the whole sky.

methods.title: The Light Source Hunt
methods.example: To find and sort the light sources in your home into natural and artificial groups. Make a Prediction: Before you start, guess: Do you think you will find more natural light sources or more artificial ones inside your home? Write down or say your guess.
steps: Walk slowly through the rooms of your home with an adult.
Look for every object that makes its own light. Remember: a light source makes light, it does not just reflect it.
Each time you find one, write it down or tell your adult to write it.
Beside each one, mark N for natural or A for artificial.
Look out of a window too, and add any light sources you see outside, such as the sun.

methods.title: Growing and Shrinking Shadows
methods.example: To find out what happens to a shadow when you move the light source closer to and farther from an object. Make a Prediction: Before you start, guess: When I move the torch closer to the object, will the shadow get bigger or smaller?
steps: Stand the toy on a table a little way from the wall.
Shine the torch at the toy so its shadow appears on the wall.
Hold the torch far from the toy. Measure the shadow with the ruler and write down its length.
Now move the torch closer to the toy. Keep the toy and wall in the same place — only move the torch.
Measure the shadow again and write down its length.

methods.title: The Bouncing Light Mirror Test
methods.example: To discover which surfaces reflect light and pictures well, and which ones do not. Make a Prediction Before you start, guess: Which surface will show your face most clearly — a mirror, a metal spoon, a bowl of water, or a piece of cloth?
steps: Place your objects on a table in a row.
Look into each one and try to see your face. Notice how clear the picture is each time.
Now shine the torch at each surface (never into your own eyes) and see how much light bounces back.
Give each surface a score from 1 (no reflection) to 5 (very clear reflection).
Gently touch the surface of the still water, then look again while it is wobbling. Notice the change.

methods.title: Day and Night with a Ball and a Torch
methods.example: To show how the spinning Earth makes day and night, using a ball as the Earth and a torch as the sun. Make a Prediction: Before you start, guess: When the torch shines on one side of the ball, what will the other side be like?
steps: Stick a small sticker on the ball. This sticker is your home town, such as Hargeisa or Mombasa.
Ask an adult to hold the torch still. The torch is the sun.
Hold the ball in front of the torch so one side is lit and the other side is dark.
Notice: the lit side is having day, and the dark side is having night.
Slowly turn the ball around, like the spinning Earth.

workedExamples.title: Measuring How Shadows Change
workedExamples.prompt: Scientists like to measure things carefully so they can spot patterns. Let us work through an example together, step by step, so you can see how a scientist thinks. Imagine Farah does a shadow experiment with a small toy camel standing on the table and a torch shining on it. He measures the length of the shadow each time he moves the torch.
workedExamples.solution:
The question: What happens to the shadow when the torch moves closer to the toy camel?

Step 1 — Set up carefully. Farah stands the toy camel on the table near a wall. He holds the torch far away at first and shines it at the camel so a shadow appears on the wall.

Step 2 — Measure the first shadow. With the torch far away, Farah measures the shadow with a ruler. The shadow is 10 centimetres long. He writes this down. Writing down what you see is an important part of doing science.

Step 3 — Change one thing. Farah moves the torch closer to the camel. He keeps the camel and the wall in the same place — he only moves the torch. Changing just one thing at a time is a smart scientist trick, because then you know exactly what caused the change.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a natural light source? a) a torch b) the sun c) a light bulb
workedExamples.solution: 1. b) the sun. The sun is made by nature, so it is a natural light source. A torch and a bulb are made by people.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these makes its OWN light? a) the moon b) a mirror c) a candle
workedExamples.solution: 2. c) a candle. A candle makes its own light with its flame. The moon and a mirror only reflect light.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: Darkness is best described as: a) a black thing that fills a room b) a place with little or no light c) a kind of cloud
workedExamples.solution: 3. b) a place with little or no light. Darkness is not a thing; it is what is left when light is missing.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: To see an object, light must: a) come out of your eyes b) bounce off the object into your eyes c) stay inside the object
workedExamples.solution: 4. b) bounce off the object into your eyes. Eyes do not send out light; they catch light that reflects off objects.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: To make a shadow you need a light, a surface, and: a) a mirror b) an opaque object c) water
workedExamples.solution: 5. b) an opaque object. An opaque object blocks the light, and the three things needed are a light, an opaque object, and a surface.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: A material that lets light pass straight through is called: a) opaque b) transparent c) shiny
workedExamples.solution: 6. b) transparent. Transparent materials, like clear glass and water, let light pass through.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: When you move a torch closer to an object, its shadow gets: a) bigger b) smaller c) disappears
workedExamples.solution: 7. a) bigger. Moving the light closer to the object makes the shadow grow larger.

activities.title: Growing and Shrinking Shadows
activities.materials: A torch or the torch on a phone (ask an adult); A small toy or a cup; A blank wall or a sheet of paper on the wall; A ruler; A darker room helps you see
steps: Stand the toy on a table a little way from the wall.
Shine the torch at the toy so its shadow appears on the wall.
Hold the torch far from the toy. Measure the shadow with the ruler and write down its length.
Now move the torch closer to the toy. Keep the toy and wall in the same place — only move the torch.
Measure the shadow again and write down its length.

activities.title: The Bouncing Light Mirror Test
activities.materials: A safe mirror (ask an adult); A shiny metal spoon; A bowl of still water; A piece of cloth or dark paper; A torch
steps: Place your objects on a table in a row.
Look into each one and try to see your face. Notice how clear the picture is each time.
Now shine the torch at each surface (never into your own eyes) and see how much light bounces back.
Give each surface a score from 1 (no reflection) to 5 (very clear reflection).
Gently touch the surface of the still water, then look again while it is wobbling. Notice the change.
Safety: Glass breaks — carry jars and mirrors with two hands, and tell an adult straight away if anything chips or cracks.

activities.title: Day and Night with a Ball and a Torch
activities.materials: A ball, an orange, or a round fruit; A torch; A small sticker or a dot drawn with pen; A darker room
steps: Stick a small sticker on the ball. This sticker is your home town, such as Hargeisa or Mombasa.
Ask an adult to hold the torch still. The torch is the sun.
Hold the ball in front of the torch so one side is lit and the other side is dark.
Notice: the lit side is having day, and the dark side is having night.
Slowly turn the ball around, like the spinning Earth.

activities.title: Observe: Reflection and Mirrors
activities.materials: A pencil and paper; Your own eyes; An adult to walk around with you
steps: Look for an example of reflection and mirrors around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Light and Light source.

rules.title: What Is Light and Where Does It Come From?
rules.text: Let us start with a big and simple idea.

rules.title: Darkness Is the Absence of Light
rules.text: Now let us think about the opposite of light: darkness.

rules.title: How We See Objects
rules.text: Here is one of the most surprising ideas in this whole unit.

rules.title: Shadows and How They Form
rules.text: Shadows are one of the most fun parts of studying light, and you can play with them almost anywhere.

rules.title: Reflection and Mirrors
rules.text: You already learned that we see objects because light bounces off them into our eyes.

rules.title: Day and Night
rules.text: Now let us put our light knowledge together to understand something that happens every single day of your life: day and night.

terms: Light
Energy that lets us see. It travels very fast in straight lines.
Light source
Something that makes its own light, like the sun, a torch, or a candle.
Natural light
Light from nature: the sun, stars, lightning, and fire.
Artificial light
Light people make: bulbs, torches, and phone screens.
Darkness
What is left when there is little or no light. Not a thing by itself.
Shadow
A dark shape made when an opaque object blocks light.
Opaque
Blocks light completely, so it makes a clear shadow (wood, stone, your body).
Transparent
Lets light pass straight through (clear glass, clean water).
Reflection
When light bounces off a surface and changes direction.
Mirror
A smooth, shiny surface that reflects light very well.
Day
The bright time when your side of Earth faces the sun.
Night
The dark time when your side of Earth faces away from the sun.

vocabulary.meaning: Energy that lets us see. It travels very fast in straight lines.
vocabulary.example: You can see all of these things because of one amazing thing called light.

vocabulary.meaning: Something that makes its own light, like the sun, a torch, or a candle.
vocabulary.example: The sun is our biggest and most important light source.

vocabulary.meaning: Light from nature: the sun, stars, lightning, and fire.
vocabulary.example: The sun, the stars, lightning, and fire give natural light.

vocabulary.meaning: Light people make: bulbs, torches, and phone screens.
vocabulary.example: Artificial light sources are made by people.

vocabulary.meaning: What is left when there is little or no light. Not a thing by itself.
vocabulary.example: Explain that we need light to see objects, and that in complete darkness we cannot see at all.

vocabulary.meaning: A dark shape made when an opaque object blocks light.
vocabulary.example: Show how a shadow forms when an object blocks light, and explain what makes a shadow bigger, smaller, or point in a different direction.

vocabulary.meaning: Blocks light completely, so it makes a clear shadow (wood, stone, your body).
vocabulary.example: A wooden door and your own body are opaque, so they make shadows.

vocabulary.meaning: Lets light pass straight through (clear glass, clean water).
vocabulary.example: Clear glass and clean water are transparent — you can see through them.

vocabulary.meaning: When light bounces off a surface and changes direction.
vocabulary.example: Explain reflection — how light bounces off smooth, shiny surfaces such as mirrors and calm water.

vocabulary.meaning: A smooth, shiny surface that reflects light very well.
vocabulary.example: You will discover where light comes from, why we cannot see in the dark, how shadows are made, and how a shiny mirror can bounce light back to your eyes.

vocabulary.meaning: The bright time when your side of Earth faces the sun.
vocabulary.example: When you wake up on the Indian Ocean coast near Mombasa or Kismaayo, the bright morning sun tells you that a new day has begun.

vocabulary.meaning: The dark time when your side of Earth faces away from the sun.
vocabulary.example: When your family lights a torch or flashlight to walk safely across the compound at night, you are using light that people made.

commonMistakes: My eyes send out light to see.
Eyes only catch light. Light bounces off objects INTO your eyes.
Darkness is only the absence of light.
The moon makes its own light.
A shadow is a dark object.
A shadow is just blocked light on a surface.
The sun moves across the sky.
The Earth spins; the sun stays put.

connections.text: Earth and Space (next unit): Day, night, the sun, the moon, and its changing shapes all grow out of what you learned here.
Many artificial light sources, like bulbs and torches, work using electricity and batteries.
Plants need light to make their food, and animals like owls and bats are specially suited to the dark.
Measuring shadow lengths and giving reflections a score uses counting and comparing.
Light safety, using lamps at night, and finding shade all use this science.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why does a mirror show a clear picture but a rough wall does not?

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is the moon NOT a light source?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 6. The moon makes no light of its own. It only reflects sunlight back to us, so it is a reflector, not a light source.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, you will be able to reach these learning goals. Read them now, and read them again at the end to see how much you have grown as a scientist.
I can name many light sources around you and say whether each one is natural or made by people.
I can explain that we need light to see objects, and that in complete darkness we cannot see at all.
I can describe what darkness is — it is not a thing by itself, it is simply what happens when light is missing or blocked.
I can show how a shadow forms when an object blocks light, and explain what makes a shadow bigger, smaller, or point in a different direction.
I can explain reflection — how light bounces off smooth, shiny surfaces such as mirrors and calm water.
I can explain day and night as the result of the sun lighting one side of the spinning Earth.
I can follow light safety rules, especially the golden rule of never looking straight at the sun.
